paragraphs.text: The Olympic Torch Beginning in 776 BC, the Greeks held the Olympic Games every four years in Olympia. Back then, the Olympic torch made a long journey before the opening ceremony of each Olympic Games. The Greek people would light a flame in a cauldron on the altar, a ritual devoted to Hera, the Greek goddess of birth and marriage.

The reintroduction of the Olympic flame occurred at the Amsterdam 1928 Games, for which a cauldron was lit, though there was no torch relay. The 1936 Berlin Summer Games featured the first Olympic torch relay, which was not introduced at the Winter Olympics until 1952. However, in that year the torch was lit not in Olympia, Greece, but in Norway, which was considered the birthplace of skiing. It was not until the 1964 Winter Olympics in Innsbruck, Austria, that the Olympic flame was reignited at Olympia.

The torch begins as an abstract concept created by a designer or a group of designers. Several design teams submit their proposals to the Olympic Committee in the hope of getting the chance to create the torch. The winning group develops a design for a torch that has both aesthetic and practical value. After the torch is completed, it must withstand all sorts of severe weather conditions. The appearance of the modern Olympic torch is attributed to Disney artist John Hench, who designed the torch for the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley, California. His design laid a solid foundation for all future Olympic torches.

The long journey to the Olympic host city is not completed by one single torch, but by thousands of them, so the torch has to be replicated many times. Approximately 10,000 to 15,000 torches are produced for the thousands of runners who take the torches through every section of the Olympic relay. Each runner can choose to buy his or her torch as a treasured souvenir when he or she finishes his or her part of the relay.

The first torch in the modern Olympics (the 1936 Berlin Games) was made from a slender steel rod with a circular platform at the top and a circular hole in the middle to emit a flame. The runner’s name was also inscribed on the platform as a token of thanks. In the earlier days, torches used everything from gunpowder to olive oil as fuels. Some torches used a combination of hexamine and naphthalene with a flammable fluid. However, these materials weren’t exactly the ideal fuel sources, and they could be quite hazardous at times. In the 1956 Olympics, the torch in the final relay was ignited by magnesium and aluminium, but some flaming pieces fell off and seared the runner’s arms.

To improve safety, liquid fuels made their first appearance at the 1972 Munich Games. Since then, torches have used fuels pressurised into liquid form. When the fuels are burnt, they turn into gas to produce a flame. Liquid fuel is safer for the runner and can be stored in a light container. The torch at the 1996 Atlanta Summer Olympics was equipped with an aluminium base that accommodated a tiny fuel tank. As the fuel rises through the modified handle, it is squeezed through a brass valve that has thousands of little openings. As the fuel passes through the tiny openings, it accumulates pressure. Once it makes its way through the openings, the pressure decreases and the liquid becomes gas so it can burn.

The torch in 1996 was fuelled by propylene, a type of substance that could produce a bright flame. However, since propylene was carbon-rich, it would produce plenty of smoke which was detrimental to the environment. In 2000, the designers of the Sydney Olympic torch proposed a lighter and cheaper design, which was harmless to the environment. As fuel, they chose a combination of 35 per cent propane (a gas that is used for cooking and heating) and 65 per cent butane (a gas that is obtained from petroleum), thus creating a powerful flame without generating much smoke.

Both the 1996 and 2000 torches used a dual-flame system, enabling the flames to stay lit even in severe weather conditions. The exterior flame burns at a slower rate and at a lower temperature. It can be perceived easily with its big orange flame, but it is unstable. On the other hand, the interior flame burns faster and hotter, generating a small blue flame with great stability, because its inner location offers protection from the wind. Accordingly, the interior flame would serve as a pilot light, which could relight the external flame if it should go out.

As for the torch at the 2002 Olympics in Salt Lake City, the top section was made of glass in which the flame burned, to reflect that Olympics’ theme, ‘Light the Fire Within’. This torch was of great significance for the design of subsequent torches.
